summary: A 1971 informational note by R. W. Watson describing an interactive network experiment to study modes of access to the Network Information Center.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC outlines an experiment on remote access to the Network Information Center's online system. It proposes comparing different ways to handle typing and feedback across the network.

which remote access modes did rfc 96 compare
subtitle: A plan to compare ways of using the Network Information Center over the network.

tldr.problem: The Network Information Center wanted to study how remote users could interact with its online system despite slow terminals and network delays.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes comparing three access approaches and several character- and line-based communication modes, while gathering response-time measurements and user impressions.
tldr.outcome: The proposed experiment was intended to guide access design for the NIC and other interactive systems.

today: RFC 96 is an Informational proposal for an experiment on remote access to the Network Information Center. It describes study plans rather than a protocol specification.

sections.title: What the Experiment Would Study
sections.content:
RFC 96 outlines an interactive experiment to study remote access to the Network Information Center (NIC). The NIC's planned online services would support creating, editing, searching, and distributing text through the SRI-ARC online system.

The experiment would examine how well remote terminals and host systems could use those services over the network. It aimed to collect response-time statistics and users' impressions, not to conduct formal productivity studies.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed experiment would test how remote users could work with the NIC's online text system. It would measure response times and collect users' views about the experience.

sections.title: Three Ways to Connect
sections.content: The memo describes three access approaches: a User Program Telnet, an NLS(T) Front End, and a Monitor Telnet. Each required software at the remote host. The front end could handle tasks such as local character echoing, command parsing, and error handling before sending a parsed command to the NIC.
sections.plainLanguage: The experiment compares three ways for a remote host to connect to the NIC. One approach moves some interaction work to a program at the remote site.

sections.title: Communication Modes and Measurements
sections.content:
The proposed tests include character-at-a-time full-duplex communication, character-at-a-time half-duplex communication, and line-at-a-time half-duplex communication. The memo also describes short and long modes for half-duplex use and proposes testing with terminals operating at 10, 15, and 30 characters per second.

It notes that character echo delays had sometimes reached four or five seconds or longer in prior experience. The experiment would compare performance and user reactions to different access modes.
sections.plainLanguage: The study would compare sending each character with sending a line or command at a time. It would measure delays and ask users which mode felt workable.

references.text: Watson, R. W., "NIC Access Conventions", NWG/RFC 97, 1971.
